name: Dinacharya

card.summary: The Ayurvedic daily routine of morning hygiene, oil pulling, tongue scraping, skin care and regular sleep, followed to support clearer skin, fresher breath and a healthy appearance.
card.note: Some Ayurvedic preparations contain heavy metals; routines of hygiene and sleep are distinct from those.

quick.overview:
Dinacharya is the daily regimen in Ayurveda, India's traditional medical system. It begins before sunrise and covers waking, cleaning the teeth and tongue, oil pulling, skin care, bathing, eye washing and a consistent sleep pattern. Followers say it keeps skin, teeth and eyes in good condition.

Research is mostly descriptive reviews and small studies, such as a review of Ayurvedic tooth-cleaning practice and a trial of an Ayurvedic face paste for hyperpigmentation. Ayurveda as a system is characterised by Wikipedia as pseudoscientific, while the hygiene practices overlap with ordinary routines.
quick.how: People adopt it as a morning and evening schedule: rise early, clean teeth with a twig or herbal powder, scrape the tongue, oil pull, apply oil to skin, bathe, and sleep at consistent times, adapted to their dosha.
quick.risks: Basic hygiene steps are low risk. Some Ayurvedic herbo-mineral preparations reportedly contain toxic levels of lead, mercury and arsenic, so these differ from routine steps.

lead: Dinacharya is the daily routine in Ayurveda: following natural cycles of waking, sleeping, working and meditating, with central attention to hygiene such as bathing, teeth cleaning, oil pulling, tongue scraping, skin care and eye washing [1][2].

For appearance, the routine bundles skin, oral and sleep habits. Ayurvedic cosmetology literature treats beauty as beginning with dinacharya, and a trial of an herbal face paste for hyperpigmentation frames its work in that tradition [3]. Reviews discuss daily regimens for insomnia and stress [4][5].
Mainstream sources describe the theory as unscientific while some of the hygiene steps resemble standard practices [1].

chain: Consistent morning and evening hygiene and sleep schedule
Cleaner mouth, cared-for skin, regular rest
Healthier-looking skin, teeth and overall freshness
angle.text: The routine packages everyday habits that influence how skin, teeth and eyes look. Followers do it to keep a regular grooming and sleep pattern.

infobox: Tooth and tongue cleaning, oil pulling, skin oiling, bathing, eye wash [1]

paras: Ayurveda teaches that natural cycles of waking, sleeping and work matter for health, and hygiene is central [1]. Dinacharya starts before sunrise and includes tooth brushing with a soft twig of medicinal plants, with or without herbal powder [2]. Ayurvedic cosmetology is described as running from dinacharya to night and seasonal regimens (ratricharya, ritucharya) [3].

Ayurveda describes three doshas, vata, pitta and kapha, whose balance is said to determine health and constitution [1]. Critics say doshas are not real, and Wikipedia describes Ayurveda's theory as pseudoscientific [1]. Indian public-health authors argue the lifestyle focus may be relevant to primary care and non-communicable disease prevention [5][6].

Followers adopt it for clear skin, oral cleanliness and steady sleep. A review of Ayurvedic tooth-cleaning practice compares it to modern oral hygiene [2], and a review of Ayurvedic insomnia treatments includes daily regimens [4].
Many Ayurvedic preparations, particularly rasashastra, reportedly contain toxic levels of lead, mercury and arsenic [1].

No studies found testing dinacharya as a whole for appearance. A 62-patient double-arm trial examined Ayurvedic preparations for hypermelanosis [3], and a 2026 protocol describes a cluster randomised trial of Ayurveda-based lifestyle advocacy [7]. Narrative reviews cover insomnia and stress [4][5].
